chunks.title: GIOŚ and air-quality measurements in Poland – unofficial English translation
chunks.location: section: GIOŚ and air-quality measurements in Poland – unofficial English translation
chunks.text:
Source: Chief Inspectorate of Environmental Protection (Główny Inspektorat Ochrony Środowiska, GIOŚ), pages "Kim
jesteśmy" (https://powietrze.gios.gov.pl/pjp/content/about_us) and "Informacje ogólne"
(https://powietrze.gios.gov.pl/pjp/content/measuring_air_assessment_measurings), read on 9 October 2026. This is an
unofficial translation of the parts about who measures the air and how; the Polish pages are the official text.

chunks.title: GIOŚ and air-quality measurements in Poland – unofficial English translation
chunks.text:
"The Inspection for Environmental Protection is established to check compliance with environmental protection law and
to study and assess the state of the environment. The Inspection consists of the Chief Inspectorate of Environmental
Protection (GIOŚ) and 16 voivodeship inspectorates of environmental protection."

"Air-quality monitoring within the State Environmental Monitoring (PMŚ) is coordinated and carried out by the Chief
Inspector of Environmental Protection, in accordance with the Act of 10 July 1991 on the Inspection for Environmental
Protection." Its aim is to obtain information and data on the levels of substances in the ambient air.

chunks.title: GIOŚ and air-quality measurements in Poland – unofficial English translation
chunks.location: section: How the air is measured
chunks.text:
- Under the Environmental Protection Law and its regulations, GIOŚ measures the concentrations of sulphur dioxide,
  nitrogen dioxide and nitrogen oxides, benzene, carbon monoxide, ozone, **particulate matter PM10 and PM2.5**, and
  lead, arsenic, cadmium, nickel and benzo(a)pyrene in PM10.
- The monitoring system is based on networks of measuring stations placed where they are needed in each voivodeship,
  mostly in cities, where analyses show high concentrations of pollutants.
- There are **288 stations** in Poland, of which **219** are automatic or automatic-manual; their **hourly** results
  are published as they come on the "Jakość Powietrza" (Air Quality) portal and in the GIOŚ mobile apps. In total there
  are about 1,800 measuring positions: about 1,050 automatic and about 750 manual.
- **Manual** measurements (filters analysed in a laboratory) are published only after about **1–1.5 months**, because
  of the laboratory procedures.

chunks.title: GIOŚ and air-quality measurements in Poland – unofficial English translation
chunks.location: section: What this means for smogcast
chunks.text:
- smogcast uses the **automatic hourly** PM10 and PM2.5 results of the stations in the 10 largest Polish cities:
  the live results for today's forecast and the yearly archive of GIOŚ (2021–2025) for learning and testing.
- Manual positions have no live hourly data, so they cannot be used for tomorrow's forecast.
- Live hourly results are preliminary; GIOŚ verifies the data later and publishes the verified results in its yearly
  archive. smogcast therefore marks measured values from the live feed as not yet verified.

chunks.title: GIOŚ: information on high concentrations of air pollutants – unofficial English translation
chunks.location: section: Recommended behaviour at the PM10 information level (100 µg/m³)
chunks.text:
In the event of a smog situation and an exceedance of the **information level for PM10 in the air (100 µg/m³)**, in
order to reduce exposure to high concentrations of air pollutants, **small children, pregnant women, older people
and people with heart or respiratory diseases are advised to limit their time outdoors. Adults without health
problems are advised to refrain from physical activity in the open air.**

chunks.title: GIOŚ: information on high concentrations of air pollutants – unofficial English translation
chunks.location: section: Recommended behaviour at the PM10 alarm level (150 µg/m³)
chunks.text:
In the event of an exceedance of the **alarm level for PM10 (150 µg/m³)**, because of the very high concentrations of
pollutants in the air, **everyone is advised to limit their time outdoors to the necessary minimum.**

chunks.title: GIOŚ: information on high concentrations of air pollutants – unofficial English translation
chunks.text:
Notices about the risk or the occurrence of an exceedance are published in the sections "Exceedances and risk of
exceedances" of the regional (voivodeship) subpages of the Air Quality portal, in the "Regional information" module.

The tabs "Information and alarm levels" and "Limit values" publish the place, time, magnitude and cause of each
exceedance in Poland of the information level, the alarm level or the limit value whose averaging period is
1 hour or 24 hours.

Particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5) and health – based on the European Environment Agency
chunks.location: section: Particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5) and health – based on the European Environment Agency
chunks.text:
Source: European Environment Agency (EEA), "How air pollution affects our health"
(https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/topics/in-depth/air-pollution/how-it-affects-our-health) and "Air quality status report
2025 – Particulate matter" (https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/publications/air-quality-status-report-2025/particulate-matter),
read on 9 October 2026. The quoted sentences are the EEA's own words; the rest is a short guide to them.

chunks.title: Particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5) and health – based on the European Environment Agency
chunks.text:
Particulate matter (PM) is dust made of tiny particles in the air. The two sizes measured in Poland are:
- **PM10** – "particulate matter with a diameter of 10 µm or less" (EEA);
- **PM2.5** – fine particulate matter, 2.5 µm or less: a part of PM10 small enough to get deep into the lungs.

In smogcast, a **smog day** means a day when the daily mean of PM10 or PM2.5 at the worst station of a city is above
the daily limit.

chunks.title: Particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5) and health – based on the European Environment Agency
chunks.text:
- "PM10 is emitted mainly by the combustion of solid fuels for domestic heating, although industrial activities,
  agriculture and road transport are also important sources." (EEA)
- "In many central and eastern European countries, solid fuels such as coal and wood are used for heating households
  and in some industrial facilities and power plants." (EEA) This is why smog in Polish cities comes mostly in the
  heating season.
- Natural sources add to it: "sea salt, Saharan dust or volcanoes", and some particles form in the air itself "as a
  combination of different gases (for instance, ammonia and nitrogen dioxide)" (EEA).
- "Residential, commercial and institutional energy consumption was the principal source of particulate matter in
  2023. The manufacturing and extractive industry and transport were also significant sources, while agriculture was an
  important source of PM10." (EEA)

chunks.title: Particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5) and health – based on the European Environment Agency
chunks.text:
- "Air pollution is the single largest environmental health risk in Europe and a major cause of premature death and
  disease." (EEA)
- "Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is the air pollutant driving the most significant health problems and premature
  mortality." (EEA) The EEA estimates that in 2023 "approximately 182,000 premature deaths were attributable to PM2.5
  in the 27 EU Member States".
- "Both short- and long-term exposure to air pollution can lead to a wide range of diseases, including stroke, chronic
  obstructive pulmonary disease, trachea, bronchus and lung cancers, aggravated asthma and lower respiratory
  infections." Long exposure "can affect every organ in the body". (EEA)
- **Who is most at risk:** "Children and adolescents are particularly vulnerable because their bodies, organs and immune
  systems are still developing." The EEA also notes that "poorer people are more likely to live next to busy roads or
  industrial areas".

chunks.title: Particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5) and health – based on the European Environment Agency
chunks.location: section: Limits and guidelines for PM10 (EEA)
chunks.text:
| | Daily | Annual |
|---|---|---|
| EU limit value | 50 µg/m³ | 40 µg/m³ |
| WHO guideline level | 45 µg/m³ | 15 µg/m³ |

"Concentrations above the EU daily limit value for PM10 are seen mainly in Italy and some eastern European countries."
(EEA)

chunks.title: Particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5) and health – based on the European Environment Agency
chunks.text: "Between 2005 and 2023, emissions of particulate matter, PM10 and PM2.5, fell by 36% and 38%, respectively." (EEA)

chunks.title: Polish air-quality levels for particulate matter (PM10, PM2.5) – unofficial English translation
chunks.location: section: Polish air-quality levels for particulate matter (PM10, PM2.5) – unofficial English translation
chunks.text:
> **Unofficial translation** prepared for the smogcast knowledge base. Only the parts concerning particulate matter
> are translated. The legally binding text is the Polish original: Regulation of the Minister of the Environment of
> 24 August 2012 on the levels of certain substances in the air (consolidated text: Journal of Laws – Dziennik Ustaw –
> 2021, item 845; https://eli.gov.pl/api/acts/DU/2021/845/text.pdf), as amended by the Regulation of 8 October 2019
> (Journal of Laws 2019, item 1931), in force since 11 October 2019. In case of doubt the Polish text prevails.

chunks.title: Polish air-quality levels for particulate matter (PM10, PM2.5) – unofficial English translation
chunks.text:
The regulation sets, among others: limit values for certain substances in the air (for the protection of human
health and of plants), target values, long-term objectives, **alarm levels** – levels whose even brief exceedance may
endanger human health, **information levels**, the exposure concentration obligation, the averaging periods of
measurement results, the permitted number of exceedances and the dates by which the levels must be attained.

- Limit values for, among others, particulate matter PM2.5 and PM10 are set in Annex 1.
- Target values (including PM2.5) are set in Annex 2.
- **Alarm levels** for nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, ozone and **particulate matter PM10** are set in Annex 4.
- **Information levels** for ozone and **particulate matter PM10** are set in Annex 5.
- Levels of particulate matter are determined under actual conditions (actual temperature and pressure).
- The regulation implements, among others, Directive 2008/50/EC on ambient air quality and cleaner air for Europe.

chunks.title: Polish air-quality levels for particulate matter (PM10, PM2.5) – unofficial English translation
chunks.location: section: Annex 1 – limit values (protection of human health)
chunks.text:
| Substance | Averaging period | Limit value | Permitted exceedances per calendar year | To be attained by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Particulate matter PM10 | 24 hours | **50 µg/m³** | **35 times** | 2005 |
| Particulate matter PM10 | calendar year | **40 µg/m³** | – | 2005 |
| Particulate matter PM2.5 | calendar year | **25 µg/m³** (phase I) | – | 1 January 2015 |
| Particulate matter PM2.5 | calendar year | **20 µg/m³** (phase II) | – | 1 January 2020 |

PM10 = concentration of dust with an aerodynamic diameter of up to 10 µm; PM2.5 = up to 2.5 µm; measured by the
gravimetric method with fraction separation or by methods recognised as equivalent.

**There is no daily (24-hour) limit value for PM2.5 in Polish law** – only annual values.

chunks.text:

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.location: section: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.text:
This document explains, for users of the smogcast assistant, what the forecast says, where its data comes from, how
the model was trained and tested, how good it is and where its limits are.

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.text:
> **Will the daily PM10 or PM2.5 limit be exceeded tomorrow in a city, and how sure is that?**

The answer is a **probability** from 0 to 100%, separately for PM10 and PM2.5, for each of the 10 largest cities in
Poland: Warszawa, Kraków, Wrocław, Łódź, Poznań, Gdańsk, Szczecin, Bydgoszcz, Lublin and Białystok. Some of them often
have smog (Kraków, Łódź), others are usually cleaner (Gdańsk, Szczecin).

The forecast is about tomorrow only: smogcast does not forecast several days ahead, and it does not forecast the
concentration itself (how many µg/m³), only whether the daily limit will be exceeded.

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.text:
| Term | Meaning in smogcast |
|---|---|
| day | a calendar day in Central European Time (CET, UTC+1 all year), the way the Chief Inspectorate of Environmental Protection (GIOŚ) computes daily means |
| daily mean of a station | the mean of its hourly results; it counts only if at least 18 of the 24 hours were measured (the EU completeness rule) |
| PM10 exceedance | a daily mean **above 50 µg/m³**, the Polish and EU limit value for health protection (35 such days a year are allowed) |
| PM2.5 exceedance | a daily mean **above 25 µg/m³**, the EU daily limit value that applies from 2030 (Polish law has no daily PM2.5 limit today) |
| exceedance in a city | **at least one** station of the city has a valid daily mean above the limit; this is how GIOŚ reports exceedances |
| smog day | a day with an exceedance in a city |
| warning | a forecast of **50% or more** |
| "how sure" | the probability, checked for **calibration**: of all days forecast at about 70%, the limit should really be exceeded on about 70% |

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.location: section: 3. Where the data comes from
chunks.text:
- **History of measurements:** the yearly archive of GIOŚ with hourly PM10 and PM2.5 results from all stations,
  **2021–2025** (five heating seasons), about 11 million hourly values. These data are verified by GIOŚ and very
  clean. The model learned from these years and was tested on them.
- **Today's measurements:** the live data of GIOŚ, fetched every hour. Before they reach the forecast they are
  cleaned: repeated readings are merged, impossible values (below 0 or above 1000 µg/m³) and empty values are set
  aside, and suspicious readings (a sensor stuck on one value, a single extreme hour, a sensor slowly drifting away
  from the other stations of the city) are flagged and not used. Nothing is dropped without a reason.
- **Weather:** weather **forecasts** from Open-Meteo. The model always gets the weather forecast for tomorrow, never
  the weather that really happened, because the real weather is not known when the forecast is made.

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.location: section: 4. How the forecast is made
chunks.text:
Every day the model looks at what is known about the air and the weather, and gives the probability of an exceedance
tomorrow:
- **the air so far:** yesterday's daily mean (the worst station and the city average), whether yesterday was already
  above the limit, the day before yesterday, and this morning's readings (00:00–11:00 CET). Smog rarely appears or
  disappears overnight, so these are the strongest clues;
- **tomorrow's weather forecast:** temperature (cold days mean more home heating), wind (calm air, below 1.5 m/s,
  keeps smoke over the city), rain (it washes dust out), humidity, pressure, clouds and sunshine;
- **the calendar:** month, weekend, heating season (October–April);
- **the city:** each city has its own typical level of pollution.

The model is a set of **decision trees** (gradient-boosted trees). Each tree asks a few yes/no questions about these
inputs, for example "was yesterday above 40 µg/m³?" or "will there be more than 8 hours of calm wind?", and the trees
together give a probability between 0% and 100%.

The forecast for a day is computed **three times on the day before**:

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.location: section: 4. How the forecast is made
chunks.text:
or "will there be more than 8 hours of calm wind?", and the trees
together give a probability between 0% and 100%.

The forecast for a day is computed **three times on the day before**:

| Run | Time (CET) | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| preliminary | about 00:30 | this morning's readings are not in yet |
| **official** | about 11:30 | the model has all its inputs; this is the forecast that is later checked against the measurements |
| update | about 17:30 | the same measurements, a newer weather forecast |

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.location: section: 5. How the model was trained and tested
chunks.text:
- **Training:** 2021–2023. **Choosing the model:** 2024. **Test:** 2025, a year the model never saw while learning.
  The years are split in time, never at random, because neighbouring days are alike.
- **The rules were fixed before training:** the model with the lowest error on 2024 is used, and five tests it must
  pass on 2025 were written down before any result was known. They were never changed after the results came in.
- **The test is honest:** in 2025 the model got the weather forecasts that really existed one day earlier, so the
  test shows how good the forecast is in real use.
- The results are reproducible: the same numbers come out on a laptop and in the cloud.

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.text:
| Test | In plain words | Required |
|---|---|---|
| Better than the calendar average? | are the probabilities better than "how often the limit was exceeded in this city in this month in past years"? | yes |
| Better than "tomorrow like today"? | does the model add something to repeating the last full day? | yes |
| Does "70%" really mean about 70%? | in every group of days with a similar forecast (at least 30 days), forecast and reality may differ by at most 15 percentage points | yes |
| Does it catch smog days? (PM10 only) | share of smog days that got a warning the day before | at least 60% |
| Are its warnings rarely false? (PM10 only) | share of warnings that were followed by smog | at least half |

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.location: section: 6. How we judge whether a forecast is good: coin toss, "tomorrow like today", the model
chunks.text:
A forecast that warns about smog is judged from **two sides**, always both:
1. **Smog days that got a warning:** out of all smog days, how many were warned about the day before? (Did we miss
   smog?)
2. **Warnings followed by smog:** out of all warnings, how many were followed by a real smog day? (Can you trust a
   warning?)

Both numbers count the same days (a warning and smog on the same day), but divide them by something different: once
by all smog days, once by all warnings. A good forecast needs both to be high. Warning every single day would catch
every smog day, but most warnings would be wrong.

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.location: section: 6. How we judge whether a forecast is good: coin toss, "tomorrow like today", the model
chunks.text:
A good forecast needs both to be high. Warning every single day would catch
every smog day, but most warnings would be wrong.

Two simple forecasts show how high the bar is:
- **A coin toss** (warn on heads): it catches about half of the smog days, but it also warns on half of the clean
  days, so only as many of its warnings are right as there are smog days in general: about 1 in 5 for PM2.5 and
  about 1 in 12 for PM10.
- **"Tomorrow like today"** (warn if the last full day was a smog day): a much stronger rival, because smog comes in
  episodes of several days. But it is always **two days late**. When the forecast is made in the morning, today is not
  over yet, so the last full day is yesterday; the forecast is for tomorrow. It therefore misses the first two days of
  every smog episode and keeps warning for two days after the smog is gone. It looks fine in long episodes (a frosty
  February), but when smog comes in short bursts of one or two days it never catches it.

**Example with one week**, smog from Monday to Thursday:

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.location: section: 6. How we judge whether a forecast is good: coin toss, "tomorrow like today", the model
chunks.text:
It looks fine in long episodes (a frosty
  February), but when smog comes in short bursts of one or two days it never catches it.

**Example with one week**, smog from Monday to Thursday:

| | Mon | Tue | Wed | Thu | Fri | Sat | Sun |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| smog | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | no | no |
| "tomorrow like today" warns | | | yes | yes | yes | yes | |
| the model warns (example) | | yes | yes | yes | yes | | |

"Tomorrow like today" warned on 2 of the 4 smog days, and 2 of its 4 warnings were right. The model in this example
warned on 3 of the 4 smog days, and 3 of its 4 warnings were right: it also reads this morning's measurements and
the weather forecast (frost, no wind), so it can warn before an episode starts.

The real results of the test year 2025 follow, separately for PM2.5 and for PM10 (all 10 cities together; one smog
day = one city on one day).

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.location: section: PM2.5 in the test year 2025: why the forecast can be trusted
chunks.text:
| PM2.5 (697 smog days) | Smog days that got a warning | Warnings followed by smog |
|---|---|---|
| coin toss | about 50% | about 19% |
| "tomorrow like today" | 388 of 697 (56%) | 388 of 702 (55%) |
| **the model** | **490 of 697 (70%)** | **490 of 667 (73%)** |

In the test year 2025 the PM2.5 model warned on 490 of the 697 smog days (70%), and 490 of its 667 warnings were
followed by smog (73%). "Tomorrow like today" warned on 388 of the 697 smog days (56%), and 388 of its 702 warnings
were followed by smog (55%). A coin toss would catch about half of the smog days, but only about 19% of its warnings
would be right. **Why the PM2.5 forecast can be trusted:** the model beats both simple forecasts on both questions,
and it passes all the tests fixed before training.

February 2025 shows the same picture: the PM2.5 model caught 172 of 210 smog days with 29 false alarms, while
"tomorrow like today" caught 158 with 39 false alarms.

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.location: section: PM10 in the test year 2025: why the forecast is less sure
chunks.text:
| PM10 (292 smog days) | Smog days that got a warning | Warnings followed by smog |
|---|---|---|
| coin toss | about 50% | about 8% |
| "tomorrow like today" | 124 of 292 (42%) | 124 of 293 (42%) |
| **the model** | 129 of 292 (44%) | 129 of 189 (68%) |

In the test year 2025 the PM10 model warned on only 129 of the 292 smog days (44%), and 129 of its 189 warnings were
followed by smog (68%). "Tomorrow like today" warned on 124 of the 292 smog days (42%), and 124 of its 293 warnings
were followed by smog (42%). **Why the PM10 forecast is less sure:** the model's warnings are usually right, but it
catches fewer than half of the smog days, below the 60% that was required, so the PM10 model does not pass.

In February 2025 "tomorrow like today" caught a few more PM10 smog days than the model (56 vs 48 of 126), but it
raised 63 false alarms against the model's 19.

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.location: section: 7. How good the forecast is (test year 2025)
chunks.text:
| | PM10 | PM2.5 |
|---|---|---|
| days / smog days | 3613 / 292 (8%) | 3627 / 697 (19%) |
| error of the probability (Brier score, lower is better): model / calendar average / "tomorrow like today" | **0.043** / 0.062 / 0.093 | **0.075** / 0.117 / 0.172 |
| how well days are ranked from safest to most dangerous (AUC, 1 = perfect) | 0.95 | 0.94 |
| Better than the calendar average? | passed | passed |
| Better than "tomorrow like today"? | passed | passed |
| Does "70%" really mean about 70%? | passed, but only just (largest gap 8.5 percentage points; it was above the limit in nearly identical model versions) | passed (7 percentage points) |
| Does it catch smog days? | **not passed** (44%, required 60%) | not applicable |
| Are its warnings rarely false? | passed (32% false) | not applicable |
| **Verdict** | **does not pass all tests** | **passes all tests** |

- Smog is a matter of the **heating season**: almost all smog days were between November and March. From May to
  September there were almost no smog days, and the model correctly gave no warnings.
- 2025 was smoggier than 2024, and the model still did better than both simple forecasts in 9 of the 10 cities.

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.location: section: 8. Why PM10 is harder to forecast than PM2.5
chunks.text:
- PM2.5 is mostly **smoke** from home stoves and traffic. It depends mainly on the **weather**, which the model knows
  from the forecast: cold means more heating, calm wind keeps the smoke over the city.
- PM10 is PM2.5 **plus coarser dust**: raised from dry streets by traffic, from building sites, soil, and sand left
  after winter. These causes are not in the weather forecast, so the model sees only part of them.
- PM10 smog days are **rarer** (about 8% of days, against 19% for PM2.5), so the model has fewer examples to learn
  from, and the 50 µg/m³ limit needs a strong episode.
- More stations measure PM10, also next to busy streets. A local jump at one station is enough for a city exceedance,
  and such jumps cannot be seen in the weather forecast.

In short: the PM10 forecast is **less sure**, not useless. It ranks days well from safest to most dangerous and its
warnings are usually right, but it misses more than half of the smog days.

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.text:
Every day the forecast is made from the latest measurements and the latest weather forecast. A city without valid
measurements for yesterday, or without a complete weather forecast for tomorrow, gets "no forecast" with the reason,
never a guessed number. After each day ends, the official forecast is compared with what was really measured, so the
live record grows day by day. It is still short (live forecasts started in October 2026); the test year 2025 is the
main evidence of quality.

chunks.title: smogcast: tomorrow's PM10 and PM2.5 forecast for the 10 largest Polish cities
chunks.text:
- The PM10 forecast does not pass all the tests (sections 6–8).
- Today's set of stations is slightly larger than in the history (new stations were opened). Because a city's value
  is its worst station, more stations can make today's values slightly higher than in the years the model learned from.
- The forecast uses measurements and the weather forecast only: no data on traffic, road conditions, building sites or
  pollution blown in from far away.
- The weather used for training was slightly more accurate than real day-ahead forecasts; the test used real day-ahead
  forecasts, so the test results are not inflated by this.
- PM2.5 uses the future EU daily limit (25 µg/m³, from 2030), because Polish law has no daily PM2.5 limit today.

(48) As established by the case law of the Court of Justice (15), Member States are not to restrict legal standing to challenge a decision of a public authority to those members of the public concerned who participated in the preceding administrative procedure to adopt that decision. In addition, any review procedure has to be fair, equitable, timely and not prohibitively expensive, and provide for adequate redress mechanisms, including injunctive relief as appropriate. Furthermore, in line with the case-law of the Court of Justice (16) access to justice is, as a minimum, to be granted to the public concerned. (49) This Directive respects the fundamental rights and observes the principles recognised in particular by the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (the ‘Charter’). Where damage to human health has occurred as a result of a violation of the national rules transposing Article 19(1) to (5) and Article 20(1) and (2) of this Directive, and that violation has been committed intentionally or negligently, Member States should ensure that the individuals affected by such violations have the right to claim and obtain compensation for that damage from the relevant competent authority. The rules on compensation, access to justice and penalties laid down in this Directive have the objective to avoid, prevent and reduce harmful effects on human health and the environment from air pollution, in line with Article 191(1) TFEU. Those rules seek to integrate into the policies of the Union a high level of environmental protection and the improvement of the quality of the environment in accordance with the principle of sustainable development as laid down in Article 37 of the Charter, and put into concrete terms the obligation to protect the right to life and to the integrity of the person and the right to healthcare laid down in Articles 2, 3 and 35 of the Charter. This Directive also contributes to the right to an effective remedy before a tribunal, as laid down in Article 47 of the Charter, in relation to the protection of human health. The penalties provided for in this Directive should be effective, proportionate and dissuasive. chunks.text: C. Siting Measurements shall be taken in urban background locations and rural background locations in accordance with Annex IV. Section 3 – Measurements of ozone precursor substances A. General Ambient air quality shall be assessed in all zones and agglomerations in accordance with the following criteria: 1. Ambient air quality shall be assessed at all locations except those listed in paragraph 2, in accordance with the criteria established by Sections B and C for the location of sampling points for fixed measurement. The principles established by Sections B and C shall also apply in so far as they are relevant in identifying the specific locations in which concentration of the relevant pollutants are established where ambient air quality is assessed by indicative measurement or modelling. 2. Compliance with the limit values directed at the protection of human health shall not be assessed at the following locations: (a) any locations situated within areas where members of the public do not have access and there is no fixed habitation; (b) in accordance with Article 2(1), on factory premises or at industrial installations

chunks.title: Directive 2008/50/EC on ambient air quality and cleaner air for Europe
chunks.text: situated within areas where members of the public do not have access and there is no fixed habitation; (b) in accordance with Article 2(1), on factory premises or at industrial installations to which all relevant provisions concerning health and safety at work apply; (c) on the carriageway of roads; and on the central reservations of roads except where there is normally pedestrian access to the central reservation. B. Macroscale siting of sampling points 1. Protection of human health (a) Sampling points directed at the protection of human health shall be sited in such a way as to provide data on the following: — the areas within zones and agglomerations where the highest concentrations occur to which the population is likely to be directly or indirectly exposed for a period which is significant in relation to the averaging period of the limit value(s), — levels in other areas within the zones and agglomerations which are representative of the exposure of the general population, (b) Sampling points shall in general be sited in such a way as to avoid measuring very small micro-environments in their immediate vicinity, which means that a sampling point must be sited in such a way

chunks.title: Directive 2008/50/EC on ambient air quality and cleaner air for Europe
chunks.text: Sampling points shall in general be sited in such a way as to avoid measuring very small micro-environments in their immediate vicinity, which means that a sampling point must be sited in such a way that the air sampled is representative of air quality for a street segment no less than 100 m length at traffic-orientated sites and at least 250 m × 250 m at industrial sites, where feasible; (c) Urban background locations shall be located so that their pollution level is influenced by the integrated contribution from all sources upwind of the station. The pollution level should not be dominated by a single source unless such a situation is typical for a larger urban area. Those sampling points shall, as a general rule, be representative for several square kilometres; (d) Where the objective is to assess rural background levels, the sampling point shall not be influenced by agglomerations or industrial sites in its vicinity, i.e. sites closer than five kilometres; (e) Where contributions from industrial sources are to be assessed, at least one sampling point shall be installed downwind of the source in the nearest residential area. Where the background concentration is not known, an

chunks.title: Directive 2008/50/EC on ambient air quality and cleaner air for Europe
chunks.text: from industrial sources are to be assessed, at least one sampling point shall be installed downwind of the source in the nearest residential area. Where the background concentration is not known, an additional sampling point shall be situated within the main wind direction; (f) Sampling points shall, where possible, also be representative of similar locations not in their immediate vicinity; (g) Account shall be taken of the need to locate sampling points on islands where that is necessary for the protection of human health. L 152/18 EN Official Journal of the European Union 11.6.2008

chunks.title: Directive 2008/50/EC on ambient air quality and cleaner air for Europe
chunks.text: 2. Protection of vegetation and natural ecosystems Sampling points targeted at the protection of vegetation and natural ecosystems shall be sited more than 20 km away from agglomerations or more than 5 km away from other built-up areas, industrial installations or motorways or major roads with traffic counts of more than 50 000 vehicles per day, which means that a sampling point must be sited in such a way that the air sampled is representative of air quality in a surrounding area of at least 1 000 km2. A Member State may provide for a sampling point to be sited at a lesser distance or to be representative of air quality in a less extended area, taking account of geographical conditions or of the opportunities to protect particularly vulnerable areas. Account shall be taken of the need to assess air quality on islands. C. Microscale siting of sampling points In so far as is practicable, the following shall apply: — the flow around the inlet sampling probe shall be unrestricted (free in an arc of at least 270°) without any obstructions affecting the airflow in the vicinity of the sampler (normally some metres away from buildings, balconies, trees and other obstacles and at least

chunks.title: Directive 2008/50/EC on ambient air quality and cleaner air for Europe
chunks.text: in an arc of at least 270°) without any obstructions affecting the airflow in the vicinity of the sampler (normally some metres away from buildings, balconies, trees and other obstacles and at least 0,5 m from the nearest building in the case of sampling points representing air quality at the building line), — in general, the inlet sampling point shall be between 1,5 m (the breathing zone) and 4 m above the ground. Higher positions (up to 8 m) may be necessary in some circumstances. Higher siting may also be appropriate if the station is representative of a large area, — the inlet probe shall not be positioned in the immediate vicinity of sources in order to avoid the direct intake of emissions unmixed with ambient air, — the sampler’s exhaust outlet shall be positioned so that recirculation of exhaust air to the sampler inlet is avoided, — for all pollutants, traffic-orientated sampling probes shall be at least 25 m from the edge of major junctions and no more than 10 m from the kerbside., The following factors may also be taken into account: — interfering sources, — security, — access, — availability of electrical power and telephone communications, — visibility of the site in

chunks.title: Directive 2008/50/EC on ambient air quality and cleaner air for Europe
chunks.text: The following factors may also be taken into account: — interfering sources, — security, — access, — availability of electrical power and telephone communications, — visibility of the site in relation to its surroundings, — safety of the public and operators, — the desirability of co-locating sampling points for different pollutants, — planning requirements., D. Documentation and review of site selection The site-selection procedures shall be fully documented at the classification stage by such means as compass-point photographs of the surrounding area and a detailed map. Sites shall be reviewed at regular intervals with repeated documentation to ensure that selection criteria remain valid over time. 11.6.2008 EN Official Journal of the European Union L 152/19

chunks.text: ANNEX IV MEASUREMENTS AT RURAL BACKGROUND LOCATIONS IRRESPECTIVE OF CONCENTRATION A. Objectives The main objectives of such measurements are to ensure that adequate information is made available on levels in the background. This information is essential to judge the enhanced levels in more polluted areas (such as urban background, industry related locations, traffic related locations), assess the possible contribution from long-range transport of air pollutants, support source apportionment analysis and for the understanding of specific pollutants such as particulate matter. It is also essential for the increased use of modelling also in urban areas. B. Substances Measurement of PM2,5 must include at least the total mass concentration and concentrations of appropriate compounds to characterise its chemical composition. At least the list of chemical species given below shall be included. SO4 2– Na+ NH4 + Ca2+ elemental carbon (EC) NO3 – K+ Cl– Mg2+ organic carbon (OC) C. Siting Measurements should be taken in particular in rural background areas in accordance with parts A, B and C of Annex III. L 152/20 EN Official Journal of the European Union 11.6.2008

Reference measurement methods 1. Reference method for the measurement of sulphur dioxide The reference method for the measurement of sulphur dioxide is that described in EN 14212:2005 ‘Ambient air quality — Standard method for the measurement of the concentration of sulphur dioxide by ultraviolet fluorescence’. 2. Reference method for the measurement of nitrogen dioxide and oxides of nitrogen The reference method for the measurement of nitrogen dioxide and oxides of nitrogen is that described in EN 14211:2005 ‘Ambient air quality — Standard method for the measurement of the concentration of nitrogen dioxide and nitrogen monoxide by chemiluminescence’. 3. Reference method for the sampling and measurement of lead The reference method for the sampling of lead is that described in Section A(4) of this Annex. Reference method for the sampling and measurement of PM2,5 The reference method for the sampling and measurement of PM2,5 is that described in EN 14907:2005 ‘Standard gravimetric measurement method for the determination of the PM2,5 mass fraction of suspended particulate matter’. 6. B. Demonstration of equivalence 1. A Member State may use any other method which it can demonstrate gives results equivalent to any of the methods referred to in Section A or, in the case of particulate matter, any other method which the Member State concerned can demonstrate displays a consistent relationship to the reference method. chunks.text: As the Netherlands pointed out when the Common Position was drawn up, the air quality in our country is strongly influenced by transboundary developments and will therefore benefit enormously from an effective European approach. The Netherlands’ main concern has been that the Directive should contain a balanced package of European and national measures, as well as realistic time limits to achieve the air quality targets. Only then will Member States be able to achieve the ambitious targets that have been set. Ambient (outdoor) air pollution Skip to main content

Ambient (outdoor) air pollution

24 October 2024

Reading time:

Key facts

Air pollution is one of the greatest environmental risks to child health

In 2019, 99% of the world’s population was living in places where the WHO air quality guidelines levels were not met.

The combined effects of ambient air pollution
            and household air pollution are associated with 6.7 million premature
            deaths annually.

Ambient (outdoor) air pollution is estimated to have caused 4.2 million premature deaths worldwide in 2019.

Some 89% of those premature deaths occurred in
            low- and middle-income countries, and the greatest number in the WHO
            South-East Asia and Western Pacific Regions.

Policies and investments supporting cleaner
            transport, energy efficient homes, power generation, industry and better
            municipal waste management would reduce key sources of outdoor air
            pollution. Access to clean household energy would also greatly reduce
            ambient air pollution in some regions.

Overview

chunks.title: WHO fact sheet: Ambient (outdoor) air pollution and health
chunks.text:
Access to clean household energy would also greatly reduce
            ambient air pollution in some regions.

Overview

Outdoor air pollution is a major environmental health problem affecting everyone in low-, middle-, and high-income countries.

Ambient (outdoor) air pollution in both cities and rural areas was estimated to cause 4.2 million premature deaths worldwide per year in 2019; this mortality is due to exposure to fine particulate matter, which causes cardiovascular and respiratory disease, and cancers.

WHO estimates that in 2019, some 68% of outdoor air pollution related premature deaths were due to ischaemic heart disease and stroke, 14% were due to  chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, 14% were due to acute lower respiratory infections, and 4% of deaths were due to lung cancers.

People living in low- and middle-income countries disproportionately experience the burden of outdoor air pollution with 89% (of the 4.2 million premature deaths) occurring in these areas. The greatest burden is found in the WHO South-East Asia and Western Pacific Regions. The latest burden estimates reflect the significant role air pollution plays in cardiovascular illness and death.

chunks.title: WHO fact sheet: Ambient (outdoor) air pollution and health
chunks.text:
The greatest burden is found in the WHO South-East Asia and Western Pacific Regions. The latest burden estimates reflect the significant role air pollution plays in cardiovascular illness and death.

Policies reducing air pollution

Addressing air pollution, which is the second highest risk factor for noncommunicable diseases , is key to protecting public health.

Most sources of outdoor air pollution are well beyond the control of individuals and this demands concerted action by local, national and regional level policy-makers working in sectors like energy, transport, waste management, urban planning and agriculture.

There are many examples of successful policies that reduce air pollution:

for industry: clean technologies that reduce industrial smokestack emissions; improved management of urban and agricultural waste, including capture of methane gas emitted from waste sites as an alternative to incineration (for use as biogas);

for energy: ensuring access to affordable clean household energy solutions for cooking, heating and lighting;

chunks.text:
mini-grids and rooftop solar power generation);

for municipal and agricultural waste management: strategies for waste reduction, waste separation, recycling and reuse or waste reprocessing, as well as improved methods of biological waste management such as anaerobic waste digestion to produce biogas, are feasible, low-cost alternatives to the open incineration of solid waste – where incineration is unavoidable, then combustion technologies with strict emission controls are critical; and

for health-care activities: putting health services on a low-carbon development path can support more resilient and cost-efficient service delivery, along with reduced environmental health risks for patients, health workers and the community. In supporting climate friendly policies, the health sector can display public leadership while also improving health service delivery.

Pollutants

Particulate matter (PM)

PM is a common proxy indicator for air pollution. There is strong evidence for the negative health impacts associated with exposure to this pollutant. The major components of PM are sulfates, nitrates, ammonia, sodium chloride, black carbon, mineral dust and water.

Carbon monoxide (CO)

chunks.title: WHO fact sheet: Ambient (outdoor) air pollution and health
chunks.text:
The major components of PM are sulfates, nitrates, ammonia, sodium chloride, black carbon, mineral dust and water.

Carbon monoxide (CO)

Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless and tasteless toxic gas produced by the incomplete combustion of carbonaceous fuels such as wood, petrol, charcoal, natural gas and kerosene.

Ozone (O 3 )

Ozone at ground level – not to be confused with the ozone layer in the upper atmosphere – is one of the major constituents of photochemical smog and it is formed through the reaction with gases in the presence of sunlight.

Nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 )

NO 2 is a gas that is commonly released from the combustion of fuels in the transportation and industrial sectors.

Sulfur dioxide (SO 2 )

SO 2 is a colourless gas with a sharp odour. It is produced from the burning of fossil fuels (coal and oil) and the smelting of mineral ores that contain sulfur.

To read more details about these pollutants and other types, please visit this page .

Air quality guidelines

chunks.title: WHO fact sheet: Ambient (outdoor) air pollution and health
chunks.text:
To read more details about these pollutants and other types, please visit this page .

Air quality guidelines

The WHO Global air quality guidelines (AQG) offer global guidance on thresholds and limits for key air pollutants that pose health risks. These guidelines are of a high methodological quality and are developed through a transparent, evidence-based decision-making process. In addition to the guideline values, the WHO Global air quality guidelines provide interim targets to promote a gradual shift from high to lower concentrations and their associated health benefits. For example, through the achievement of interim target one (35 µg/m 3 ), around 300 000 deaths would be saved worldwide annually.

The guidelines also offer qualitative statements on good practices for the management of certain types of particulate matter (PM), for example black carbon/elemental carbon, ultrafine particles, and particles originating from sand and dust storms, for which there is insufficient quantitative evidence to derive AQG levels.

WHO response

chunks.title: WHO fact sheet: Ambient (outdoor) air pollution and health
chunks.text:
WHO response

Recognizing the gravity and urgency of the problem, all WHO Member States approved resolution A68.8, “Health and the Environment: addressing the health impact of air pollution,” at the World Health Assembly in 2015, complemented by a road map for action the following year.

WHO, as the coordinating authority on international health, supports countries in protecting public health through evidence-based policies and actions. Considering the significant health burden and the multiple potential benefits of interventions, WHO supports countries by providing evidence, building institutional capacity and leveraging the health argument to convene sectors to tackle air pollution.

To support reducing air pollution levels and to protect populations from health

risks, WHO’s Air Quality and Health Unit works in three cross-cutting areas:

1. knowledge, evidence and measuring progress

2. institutional capacity building and technical support

3. leadership and coordination.

Member States and sub-national entities are typically responsible for the implementation and

monitoring of policies to promote air quality for health. Successful policies

chunks.title: WHO fact sheet: Ambient (outdoor) air pollution and health
chunks.text:
Member States and sub-national entities are typically responsible for the implementation and

monitoring of policies to promote air quality for health. Successful policies

and solid governance depend on coordinated action between a variety of stakeholders and sec-

tors. Cooperation with other UN agencies and non-state actors is essential and is integrated

into WHO’s work to ensure synergies and maximize impact on the ground.

A full list of WHO’s activities to combat ambient air pollution can be found here and here .

chunks.title: smogcast result tables: what each column means
chunks.text:
Result table forecast_tomorrow: Tomorrow's PM10 / PM2.5 limit-exceedance forecast per city – always the newest run of the day.
Columns:
- city_id: City identifier (e.g. krakow).
- city_name: City name.
- jurisdiction_code: Voivodeship code (ISO 3166-2:PL, e.g. PL-12 = Małopolskie); row-level security filters on it.
- pollutant: PM10 or PM2.5.
- issue_day: Day D (CET) on which the forecast was issued.
- target_day: Day D+1 (CET) the forecast is for.
- probability: Probability (0–1) that the daily mean of the city's worst station exceeds the daily limit on target_day.
- warned: True when probability >= 0.5 – a yes/no summary of the probability.
- limit_ug_m3: Daily limit that defines an exceedance, µg/m³ (PM10 50, PM2.5 25).
- status: ok, or no_forecast when the inputs were incomplete (see unusable_reason) – never a guessed value.
- unusable_reason: Why there is no forecast (e.g. no valid PM yesterday, incomplete weather forecast); empty when status = ok.
- model: Model that produced the probability (gbt = gradient-boosted trees, chosen on the validation year).
- model_version: Saved model version used (final = refit on 2021–2024).
- weather_source: Weather forecast feed used for tomorrow's inputs (live = Open-Meteo forecast).
- pm_d1_max_ug_m3: Yesterday's highest station daily mean in the city, µg/m³ – a main reason for the forecast.
- pm_d_morning_max_ug_m3: This morning's highest station mean (00–10 CET), µg/m³.
- t_mean_c: Forecast mean temperature tomorrow, °C (cold → more home heating).
- wind_mean_ms: Forecast mean wind speed tomorrow, m/s (wind disperses dust).
- calm_hours: Forecast hours tomorrow with wind below 1.5 m/s (calm air keeps smoke over the city).
- precip_sum_mm: Forecast precipitation tomorrow, mm (rain washes dust out).
- run_kind: preliminary (before 11:30 CET, morning incomplete), official (first run from 11:30 CET – the one verified against reality) or update (later run, newer weather).
- run_id: Id of the Job run that issued the row.
- issued_at: When the forecast was computed (UTC).

chunks.title: smogcast result tables: what each column means
chunks.text:
Result table forecast_history: Every forecast run (preliminary, official, update) – how a forecast changed during the day; verify the official one.
Columns:
- city_id: City identifier (e.g. krakow).
- city_name: City name.
- jurisdiction_code: Voivodeship code (ISO 3166-2:PL, e.g. PL-12 = Małopolskie); row-level security filters on it.
- pollutant: PM10 or PM2.5.
- issue_day: Day D (CET) on which the forecast was issued.
- target_day: Day D+1 (CET) the forecast is for.
- probability: Probability (0–1) that the daily mean of the city's worst station exceeds the daily limit on target_day.
- warned: True when probability >= 0.5 – a yes/no summary of the probability.
- limit_ug_m3: Daily limit that defines an exceedance, µg/m³ (PM10 50, PM2.5 25).
- status: ok, or no_forecast when the inputs were incomplete (see unusable_reason) – never a guessed value.
- unusable_reason: Why there is no forecast (e.g. no valid PM yesterday, incomplete weather forecast); empty when status = ok.
- model: Model that produced the probability (gbt = gradient-boosted trees, chosen on the validation year).
- model_version: Saved model version used (final = refit on 2021–2024).
- weather_source: Weather forecast feed used for tomorrow's inputs (live = Open-Meteo forecast).
- pm_d1_max_ug_m3: Yesterday's highest station daily mean in the city, µg/m³ – a main reason for the forecast.
- pm_d_morning_max_ug_m3: This morning's highest station mean (00–10 CET), µg/m³.
- t_mean_c: Forecast mean temperature tomorrow, °C (cold → more home heating).
- wind_mean_ms: Forecast mean wind speed tomorrow, m/s (wind disperses dust).
- calm_hours: Forecast hours tomorrow with wind below 1.5 m/s (calm air keeps smoke over the city).

chunks.title: smogcast result tables: what each column means
chunks.text:
Result table measured_daily: What was really measured: daily PM10 / PM2.5 per city and day – GIOŚ archive 2021–2025 and the live feed (finished days only).
Columns:
- city_id: City identifier (e.g. krakow).
- city_name: City name.
- jurisdiction_code: Voivodeship code (ISO 3166-2:PL); row-level security filters on it.
- pollutant: PM10 or PM2.5.
- day_cet: Calendar day in CET (UTC+1 all year), as GIOŚ computes daily means.
- heating_season: Heating season the day belongs to, e.g. 2024/25 = October 2024 – April 2025; empty from May to September.
- max_station_mean_ug_m3: Daily mean of the city's worst station, µg/m³ – compared with the limit.
- mean_station_mean_ug_m3: Average of the stations' daily means, µg/m³.
- n_stations: Stations with a valid day (at least 18 of 24 hourly results).
- limit_ug_m3: Daily limit, µg/m³ (PM10 50, PM2.5 25).
- exceeded: True when the worst station's daily mean is above the limit – an exceedance day.
- source: archive (GIOŚ verified data 2021–2025) or live (GIOŚ API, not yet verified by GIOŚ).
- computed_at: When the table was computed (UTC).

chunks.title: smogcast result tables: what each column means
chunks.text:
Result table forecast_verification: Did the official forecast come true? Each official forecast next to what was measured on its target day.
Columns:
- city_id: City identifier (e.g. krakow).
- city_name: City name.
- jurisdiction_code: Voivodeship code (ISO 3166-2:PL); row-level security filters on it.
- pollutant: PM10 or PM2.5.
- issue_day: Day D (CET) on which the official forecast was issued.
- target_day: Day D+1 (CET) the forecast was for.
- probability: Forecast probability (0–1) of an exceedance on target_day.
- warned: True when probability >= 0.5 (a warning was issued).
- limit_ug_m3: Daily limit, µg/m³ (PM10 50, PM2.5 25).
- status: ok, or no_forecast when the inputs were incomplete.
- issued_at: When the official forecast was computed (UTC).
- measured_max_ug_m3: Measured daily mean of the city's worst station on target_day, µg/m³.
- exceeded: True when the limit was really exceeded on target_day.
- measured_source: Where the measurement comes from: live (GIOŚ API) or archive.
- outcome: hit (warned, exceeded), miss (not warned, exceeded), false_alarm (warned, not exceeded), correct_no_warning, no_forecast, no_data (no valid measurement) or pending (target day not over yet).
- squared_error: (probability − outcome)² – its average over days is the live Brier score; lower is better.
- computed_at: When the table was computed (UTC).

chunks.title: smogcast result tables: what each column means
chunks.text:
Result table backtest_predictions: Model and baseline probabilities vs what really happened, per day of the validation (2024) and test (2025) years.
Columns:
- model: gbt, logistic, or a baseline: persistence ('tomorrow like today'), climatology (calendar average).
- split: validation (2024, used to choose the model) or test (2025, never seen before the final check).
- city_id: City identifier.
- pollutant: PM10 or PM2.5.
- issue_day: Day D the forecast would have been issued.
- target_day: Day D+1 it was for.
- probability: Forecast probability of an exceedance (0–1).
- label: 1 if the limit was really exceeded on target_day, else 0.
- warned: True when probability >= 0.5.

chunks.title: smogcast result tables: what each column means
chunks.text:
Result table backtest_metrics: How good each model and baseline was, per split, pollutant and city (city_id = ALL: all cities together).
Columns:
- model: gbt, logistic, persistence or climatology.
- split: validation (2024) or test (2025).
- pollutant: PM10 or PM2.5.
- city_id: City identifier, or ALL for all cities together.
- n_days: Days evaluated.
- n_exceed: Days with a real exceedance.
- base_rate: Share of days with an exceedance.
- brier: Brier score – mean squared error of the probability; lower is better (0 = perfect).
- hits: Exceedance days with a warning.
- misses: Exceedance days without a warning.
- false_alarms: Warnings on days without an exceedance.
- brier_climatology: Brier score of the calendar-average baseline on the same days.
- auc: How well days are ranked from safest to most dangerous; closer to 1 is better.
- bss: Brier skill score vs climatology; above 0 = better than the calendar average.
- pod: Probability of detection – share of exceedance days that got a warning; higher is better.
- far: False alarm ratio – share of warnings that were false; lower is better; empty when there were no warnings.
- csi: Critical success index – hits / (hits + misses + false alarms); higher is better.

chunks.title: smogcast result tables: what each column means
chunks.text:
Result table reliability: Calibration: within each band of forecast probability, how often an exceedance really happened (does '70%' mean 70%?).
Columns:
- model: Model or baseline.
- split: validation or test.
- pollutant: PM10 or PM2.5.
- bin: Band index 0–9 (0 = forecasts 0–10%, 9 = forecasts 90–100%).
- n_days: Days in the band (bands with fewer than 30 days are not judged).
- mean_probability: Mean forecast probability in the band.
- observed_frequency: How often an exceedance really happened in the band.
- bin_from: Lower edge of the band.
- bin_to: Upper edge of the band.
- gap: observed_frequency − mean_probability; criterion K3 allows at most 0.15.

chunks.title: smogcast result tables: what each column means
chunks.text:
Result table acceptance: Verdict of the acceptance criteria K1–K4, fixed before training, for each pollutant's operational model on the 2025 test year.
Columns:
- pollutant: PM10 or PM2.5.
- model: Operational model judged.
- criterion: K1 beats climatology, K2 beats persistence, K3 calibrated, K4a catches smog days, K4b few false alarms (K4 for PM10 only).
- description: The criterion in words.
- value: Value reached on the test year.
- threshold: Value required.
- passed: True if the criterion is met.

chunks.title: smogcast result tables: what each column means
chunks.text:
Result table model_selection: Hyper-parameter grid evaluated on the validation year; operational = the model used for forecasts (lowest validation Brier).
Columns:
- pollutant: PM10 or PM2.5.
- model: gbt or logistic.
- params: Hyper-parameters of the variant (JSON).
- validation_brier: Brier score on the validation year 2024; lower is better.
- best_of_type: True for the best variant of its model type.
- operational: True for the model that produces the forecasts.

chunks.title: smogcast result tables: what each column means
chunks.text:
Result table dq_summary: Data quality of the live stream per source (live = GIOŚ API, fault_replay = demonstration with injected faults).
Columns:
- source: live or fault_replay.
- metric: records_received, unique_readings, resent_duplicates, late_rejected, quarantined[_<reason>], silver_readings, silver_valid, flag_<ok|frozen|spike|drift>.
- value: Count for the metric.
- pct_of_unique: Share of unique readings, %.
- computed_at: When the summary was computed (UTC).
